title: Perl Exercises
description: Read each example in its lesson first. Predict the result, then check your answer. The notes explain the idea and one common mistake.

exercises.question: say prints text and adds a newline. The feature line enables it. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: say writes the string and supplies a newline. The feature declaration enables say. Keep use feature "say" when using say on these versions.

exercises.question: A scalar keeps one value. Its name starts with $. my declares the variable. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: my declares a local scalar holding 3. Numeric addition returns 5. Declare variables with my when strict is enabled.

exercises.question: Double-quoted strings insert scalar variables into text. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: Double quotes allow $name to expand to Ravi. Single quotes keep the dollar text literal.

exercises.question: An array name starts with @. Read one item with $ and its zero-based position. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The whole list uses @pets, but $pets[1] selects the one value dog. Use $pets[1] for one item, not @pets[1].

exercises.question: A hash pairs keys with values. Curly braces select a value by key. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The hash associates title with Moon Trip. Curly braces read that entry. A whole hash uses %, but one selected value uses $.

exercises.question: if runs a block when the test is true. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The score passes the condition. The first branch prints Pass. Use braces around the selected steps.

exercises.question: eq compares text. == is the numeric comparison operator. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: eq compares the letters in two strings. Both are cat, so Yes is selected. Using == for words can cause unwanted number conversion.

exercises.question: for can visit each value in a list. The loop variable holds the current value. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The range includes both ends. $n receives 1, 2 and 3 on successive passes. The range 1..3 includes both ends.

exercises.question: A subroutine is a named set of steps. @_ holds its inputs. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The input assignment reads the first value in @_. return sends back twice that value. Copy the input from @_ before using it.

exercises.question: A regular expression describes a pattern. =~ asks whether the string matches it. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The ^c pattern requires c at the start. cat matches. ^ means the start, so c must be the first character.

exercises.question: s/old/new/ replaces matching text. The g flag replaces all matches. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The g flag makes replacement repeat for every match. Both red words become blue. Without g, only the first match is replaced.

exercises.question: split breaks text at a pattern. join puts a list together with a separator. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: split creates two words at the comma. join places a plus separator between them. The separator used by split is a pattern, not always plain text.
